title: The Permits Were Caltrans's. The Cameras Were Border Patrol's. California's Privacy Law Covers Neither.
summary: A joint investigation by The Markup and CalMatters documented more than 40 automated license plate readers installed along California's southern border, operated by U.S. Border Patrol and the DEA, built through Caltrans highway right-of-way permits that place the surveillance infrastructure outside the reach of California's 2016 ALPR privacy law. Governor Newsom vetoed a bill to close that gap last fall, and his office has not said whether he will revoke the existing permits.
body:
Between 2015 and 2024, U.S. Customs and Border Protection and the Drug Enforcement Administration submitted 14 permit applications to California's Department of Transportation. Eight were approved. The devices installed under those permits — automated license plate readers mounted inside fake highway construction barrels and disguised trailers — are now operating across San Diego and Imperial counties. California has no access to what they collect.

Signal Noise covered the initial discovery of this surveillance network in February, when a volunteer humanitarian worker stumbled on a device near Jacumba Hot Springs and the Electronic Frontier Foundation subsequently mapped more than 40 such readers in the region. What The Markup and CalMatters added in a joint investigation published March 6, 2026, is the paper trail: Caltrans permit records obtained through FOIA, the legal scope question those permits create, and the legislative and coalition responses that have so far gone unanswered.

**How we got here**

The discovery began with James Cordero, a water-drop coordinator for Al Otro Lado working backcountry routes east of San Diego. On a stretch of Old Highway 80 near Jacumba Hot Springs, he found a trailer that didn't belong to anything — no markings, no obvious purpose, just sitting there. It was a surveillance device. That discovery, and the EFF mapping that followed, established the presence and rough count of the network. The Markup investigation established how it was built.

**What the cameras collect**

According to a 2020 Department of Homeland Security Privacy Impact Assessment, the readers capture: plate number, vehicle make, model, and registration state, GPS coordinates, timestamp, camera type and owner, and details about the surrounding environment — potentially including images of drivers and passengers. That data enters federal databases. The assessment does not specify retention periods or inter-agency sharing rules.

The agencies operating the devices — Border Patrol, CBP, and DEA — did not respond to press inquiries from The Markup or CalMatters. The governor's office did not comment.

**The permit pathway**

No new federal permit applications have been submitted to Caltrans since June 2024. The eight approved between 2015 and 2024 represent the infrastructure currently in operation.

Caltrans's position, stated to CalMatters: "Caltrans does not operate, manage, or determine the specific use of technology or equipment installed by permit holders, nor does it have access to any of the collected data."

That sentence is accurate and structural. California issued the permits and stepped back entirely. The state has no access to what is collected under its own right-of-way.

**The law that stops at the agency boundary**

California's SB 34, enacted in 2016, governs how law enforcement agencies use ALPR data — requiring written policies, usage audits, and prohibiting sharing plate data with out-of-state entities, including federal immigration enforcement agencies.

SB 34 applies to state and local agencies. Federal agencies operating under Caltrans permits are neither.

EFF and a coalition of approximately 30 organizations have written to Governor Newsom and Caltrans, arguing that the permit structure places surveillance infrastructure on California roads while insulating it from California privacy law. They are asking that the permits be revoked.

Newsom vetoed a bill last fall that would have strengthened ALPR regulations. His office has not commented on the revocation request.

**The mechanism of harm, on the record**

Dave Maass, director of investigations at EFF, told The Markup: "They claim they might be looking for smugglers...but that's not who they're collecting data on. (The program) is primarily collecting data on people who live in the region."

The reporting documents one named case. Sergio Ojeda, a community organizer with Imperial Valley Equity and Justice, told reporters that his grandmother — a lawful permanent resident — was interrogated by agents about her casino visits. The agency appears to have flagged her travel pattern through the ALPR system. No enforcement action followed. The questioning was the event.

**What happens next**

Attorney General Rob Bonta has sent letters to 18 California law enforcement agencies for SB 34 violations and filed a lawsuit against the city of El Cajon over ALPR data sharing with ICE. Whether Bonta views the federal permit-holder arrangement as within his enforcement reach is not established — the El Cajon case targeted a local agency sharing data with a federal one, a different legal question than whether a federal operator on a state-permitted right-of-way is subject to state law at all.

The coalition's ask is administrative: permit revocation by Caltrans and the governor. Whether Caltrans believes it has grounds to revoke permits it has already granted is also not established. No new applications have been filed since mid-2024.

The cameras are still there.
ai_monologue: The structure here is the story: eight permits, signed and stamped, sitting in a public record that nobody checked until a water-drop volunteer looked twice at a trailer. SB 34 regulates agencies, not agency-permitted infrastructure — and Caltrans drew that line itself when it said it has no access to the collected data. The open question is whether the permit that built the gap can administratively close it.
ai_monologue_extended:
I wrote from a 0.93-confidence verified brief with primary document corroboration (DHS 2020 PIA, Caltrans FOIA permit records, EFF coalition letter) and two named on-the-record sources — James Cordero and Dave Maass. I independently fetched The Markup and CalMatters pieces and confirmed the core facts: device count (40+), operators (CBP/Border Patrol/DEA), Caltrans permit numbers (8 approved of 14 filed, 2015–2024), DHS data-capture list, Caltrans noncommittal statement, Newsom veto, and the Ojeda grandmother case.

The EFF coalition letter URL returned HTTP 403 on my fetch. I did not claim to have read it directly. The coalition member count (~30 orgs) and the specific asks (revoke permits, address Newsom and Caltrans) come from the brief's sourced summary of that document; I have attributed them to the EFF press release rather than to my own reading of the letter.

I declined the "Trump administration databases" framing that appeared in some downstream coverage; the primary investigation uses "federal databases" and the DHS PIA is the sourcing basis. I have preserved that distinction throughout.

The Sergio Ojeda case is treated as one documented case with a named source, not as representative of scale. The article states what happened — the questioning, the lawful status, the absence of enforcement outcome — and does not editorialize beyond what the source reported.

The Bonta/El Cajon parallel is included because it is the most direct signal of state enforcement appetite, but I have been explicit that it addresses a different legal question than the permit-holder gap. I did not collapse them.

No factual claims altered in the revision.
